subject: ela
description: Students trace and evaluate the argument and the specific claims an author makes in an informational text. They first identify the author's overall position or central claim, then locate the smaller claims the author advances to support it. For each claim they decide whether the author backs it with reasons and evidence (facts, examples, statistics, expert testimony, logical reasoning) or whether the claim is left unsupported, resting on opinion, bias, emotional appeal, or assertion alone. Students distinguish a reason (the why behind a claim) from evidence (the concrete proof) and judge how relevant and sufficient the support is. Because this is a reading standard, every item embeds the full passage or excerpt it depends on, so the student needs nothing external to answer.
subSkills: Identify the author's overall argument or central position in an informational text
Locate the specific claims the author makes to advance that argument
Distinguish a claim (a statement the author wants the reader to accept) from a reason or a piece of evidence
Distinguish a reason (the logic for why a claim is true) from evidence (the concrete facts, examples, or data that prove it)
Determine whether a given claim is supported by reasons and evidence or is left unsupported
Match a specific claim to the reason or evidence the author provides for it
Evaluate the quality of the support: judge whether the evidence is relevant to the claim and whether there is enough of it
Recognize unsupported moves such as opinion stated as fact, emotional appeal, biased language, or sweeping generalization that lacks proof

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the central argument
problemArchetypes.example: Read the short argumentative passage embedded in the item, then state the author's overall position: 'What is the main argument the author makes in this passage?' Answer names the position the author wants the reader to accept, not just the topic the passage is about.

problemArchetypes.name: Locate a specific claim
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage, then pick out one of the author's claims: 'Which sentence states a claim the author is trying to prove?' Answer points to a statement the author wants accepted, as opposed to a neutral fact or a piece of supporting evidence.

problemArchetypes.name: Distinguish claim from reason from evidence
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage, then sort the parts of the argument: 'Which of the following is evidence the author uses, not a claim?' Answer separates the concrete proof (a statistic, example, or fact) from the claim it is meant to support and from the reasoning that links them.

problemArchetypes.name: Match a claim to its support
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage, then connect a claim to the support the author gives for it: 'Which detail does the author use to support the claim that recess improves learning?' Answer names the specific reason or evidence the author offers for that one claim.

problemArchetypes.name: Judge whether a claim is supported or unsupported
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage, then evaluate one claim: 'Is the author's claim that the new schedule is unfair supported by evidence in the passage, or is it left unsupported?' Answer decides whether reasons and evidence back the claim and explains what is or is not provided.

problemArchetypes.name: Evaluate the quality of the evidence
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage, then judge how well the support fits the claim: 'Does the evidence the author gives actually prove the claim, and is there enough of it?' Answer evaluates whether the evidence is relevant and sufficient, or whether it is off-topic, too thin, or merely an opinion dressed up as proof.

problemArchetypes.name: Spot the unsupported or weak move
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage, then find the part of the argument that lacks real support: 'Which claim does the author make without backing it up with reasons or evidence?' Answer identifies the assertion that rests on opinion, feeling, biased wording, or a sweeping generalization rather than proof.

Easy.description: A short, plainly written argumentative passage (roughly 80 to 130 words) that states one clear position and offers a small number of clearly marked claims with obvious support, embedded in the item. The task is to identify: the author's overall argument, one claim, or one clearly stated piece of evidence, or to decide whether a single obvious claim is supported. The answer is stated or strongly signaled on the surface; little inference is required.
constraints: Stimulus is one short, single-position argumentative passage (about 80 to 130 words) included in the prompt
The author's position and supporting evidence are stated explicitly and plainly
Identify-level task: name the argument, point to a claim, name one piece of evidence, or decide if an obvious claim is supported
The link between claim and evidence is direct; no multi-step inference needed

Medium.description: A moderately complex argumentative passage (roughly 150 to 250 words) that advances a position through two or more claims, some well supported and at least one weakly supported or unsupported, embedded in the item. The task requires analysis: match a claim to the specific reason or evidence behind it, distinguish a reason from evidence, or determine which of several claims lacks support. The answer is grounded in the text but not stated word for word.
constraints: Stimulus is a multi-paragraph argumentative passage (about 150 to 250 words) included in the prompt
Mixes supported and unsupported claims so the student must compare them
Analyze-level task: match a claim to its support, separate reason from evidence, or find which claim is unsupported
Some inference required; the strength of the support must be weighed, not just read off the surface

Hard.description: A longer or more layered argumentative passage (roughly 280 to 420 words) that builds a position through several claims, blends solid evidence with opinion, emotional appeal, or biased language, and may include a counter-point, embedded in the item. The task requires evaluation and synthesis: trace the whole argument, judge whether the overall case is well supported, evaluate the relevance and sufficiency of the evidence, or explain why a specific claim fails despite sounding persuasive. Requires sustained inference across multiple parts of the text.
constraints: Stimulus is a longer argumentative passage (about 280 to 420 words) included in the prompt
Builds the argument through several claims and mixes genuine evidence with opinion, appeal, or bias
Evaluate or synthesize task: trace the full argument, judge overall support, weigh relevance and sufficiency of evidence, or explain why a persuasive-sounding claim is unsupported
Requires inference that draws on evidence from several places in the passage

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the topic of the passage with the author's argument, naming what the text is about instead of the position the author takes
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an answer that states the subject of the passage rather than the claim the author wants the reader to accept

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student cannot tell a claim apart from the evidence that supports it, treating a fact or statistic as if it were the claim
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a piece of evidence (a statistic, fact, or example) and labels it as the author's claim, or selects a claim and calls it the evidence

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes any claim that appears in the text must be supported simply because the author asserts it confidently
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an answer that says a claim is supported when the passage actually offers only opinion, feeling, or repetition and no real reasons or evidence

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student counts an emotional appeal or strong, biased wording as if it were factual evidence
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Identifies a sentence meant to stir feeling or persuade through loaded language as the evidence that proves the claim

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student matches a claim to a true detail from the text that does not actually support that particular claim
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks a fact that appears in the passage but is irrelevant to the specific claim the question asks about

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student judges a claim as well supported based on the amount of text rather than the relevance or sufficiency of the evidence
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an answer that calls a claim well supported because the author writes a lot about it, even though the evidence given does not actually prove the point

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats a reason (the logic for why a claim holds) as interchangeable with evidence (the concrete proof), or vice versa
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects the author's stated reasoning and labels it as evidence, or labels a concrete fact as the reason, blurring the two

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student evaluates whether the claim is true in real life instead of whether the author supported it within the passage
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an answer that judges the claim by outside knowledge or personal agreement rather than by the support the text itself provides
